29_marg618: Jerome. Solomon was called by three names: that is, Peaceable, and Jedidiah, that is, Beloved of the Lord, because in his reign there was peace and the Lord loved him; and Coheleth, that is, Ecclesiastes in Greek, one who gathers an assembly, that is, the Church: that is, a preacher, whose speech is not to one but to all. According to the three names he composed three volumes: the Proverbs, teaching little ones (whence he speaks often as if to a son); Ecclesiastes, for those of ripe age, showing that all the things we see are brief and perishing; the Canticle of Canticles, where he joins the bride, made perfect, to the embraces of the bridegroom. For unless we have left our vices and, renouncing mortal pomp, have prepared ourselves for the coming of Christ, we shall not truly say: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth.” In nearly this order the philosophers teach: first ethics, then physics, and him whom they see to have made progress in these they lead on to theology. It is to be noted too that the title differs in these. In the Proverbs: “The parables of Solomon, the son of David, king of Israel.” In Ecclesiastes: “The words of Ecclesiastes, the son of David, king of Jerusalem.” In some copies, Greek as well as Latin, “of Israel” is found added, but wrongly. In the Canticle of Canticles, neither “son of David” nor “king of Israel” or “of Jerusalem”, but only “The Canticle of Canticles of Solomon”. For so the Proverbs, as a rough instruction, belong to the twelve tribes and to all Israel; and as contempt of the world befits only the citizens of the mother city, that is, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, so the Canticle of Canticles belongs properly to those who desire only the things above. For beginners and those making progress there is both the father’s dignity and the authority of his own kingdom; but for the perfect, who do not fear but love, the name alone suffices: he is a master on a level with them and does not know that he is king.
29_marg619: How this book is to be read and expounded he says thus: Ecclesiastes is properly called “the preacher”. In an assembly a sentence is put forward by which the sedition of a tumultuous crowd is checked, and when many think diverse things they are brought to one sentence by the reasoning of the one who addresses them. This book, then, is called the preacher because in it Solomon takes up the mind of a tumultuous crowd, so as to say by way of inquiry the things which an unskilled mind perhaps feels by way of temptation. For as many opinions as he raises by inquiry, so many persons he takes upon himself; but the preacher, as with outstretched hand, calms the tumult of all and calls them back to one sentence when at the end he says: “Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse. Fear God, and keep his commandments: for this is all man.” And in saying “Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse” he hints that he has not spoken alone. There are, then, some things in this book which are raised by inquiry, others which give satisfaction by reason; some which he utters from a mind tempted and still given to the world, others in which he discusses the things of reason and restrains the mind from delight. For he says: “This therefore hath seemed good to me, that a man should eat and drink”, etc.; and afterwards: “It is better to go to the house of mourning, than to the house of feasting.” The one is in the person of the weak, the other from reason. Likewise, setting out the divers temptations of the thoughts, he says: “The death of man and of beasts is one”, etc.; “What hath the wise man more than the fool? … but to go thither where there is life.” Let the reader look carefully at these persons, lest he fall into the teaching of Epicurus.
29_marg620: The Hebrews hand down that this book is Solomon’s, doing penance because, trusting in his wisdom and riches, he offended God through women. For he will reckon with himself that all things are vain, and that those who put their hope in them come to misery.

For he himself is the Word and the Wisdom; he is rich and poor, he is the King of glory, mighty; he speaks the words to the men of the Church, to the apostles. 29_marg625: “All things are vanity: every man living.” How much more the rest? Whence: “The creature was made subject to vanity, not willingly, but by reason of him that made it subject, in hope.” For whatever is able not to be can be called vanity, because it can be changed. God alone is always the same that he is; but what is changed in some way vanishes and is not what it was. In comparison with the Creator every creature can be called vanity and counted as nothing.
29_marg626: If all things that God made are very good, how are they vanity, and even vanity of vanities? That, as in the Canticle of Canticles a song excelling among all songs is shown, so here the greatness of vanity might be displayed. Likewise in the Psalm: “All things are vanity: every man living.” If the living is vanity, then the dead is vanity of vanities. But we can say that heaven, earth and the rest are good indeed in themselves, but compared with God are as nothing; as a lamp in comparison with the sun is not seen to shine, and the lights of the stars are darkened when the sun has risen. So, looking on the elements and the manifold variety of things, I wonder indeed at the multitude of the works; but, thinking again that all things pass and grow old towards their end, and that God alone is always the same that he was, I am driven to say not once but twice: vanity of vanities, and all is vanity.

29_marg631: The Sun of justice both rises for the good and sets for the wicked, and his rising draws us to the Father. For he came for this, to raise us from earth to heaven and to say: “I, if I be lifted up from the earth, will draw all things to myself.” Nor is it strange that the Son should draw believers to himself, when the Father too draws to him: “No man can come to me, except the Father, who hath sent me, draw him.” This sun set for Jacob as he went out from his own land, and again rose for him when he entered the land of promise from Syria; and for Lot, when, having gone out from Sodom, he came to the city to which he had been unready to hasten, he went up into the mountain, and the sun rose upon Segor. Otherwise: the sun, when it runs through the south, is nearer the earth; when through the north, higher. Perhaps to those who are pinched by the cold of winter and tribulation (for “from the north shall evils break forth upon the earth”) this Sun of justice is nearer; but from those who are under the north wind, deprived of summer heat, he goes far off, and returns through his circuits to where he set out. For when he has drawn all things to himself and lit up all with his rays, there comes the restoration of the beginning, and God is all in all. Symmachus renders it thus: It goes to the south, and circles to the north; going round, the wind goes, and the wind returns through the places it had circled.
29_marg632: The sun is Christ, who quickens all things and enlightens them with the splendour and power of spiritual grace, who rises for the faithful and sets for the unbeliever.
29_marg633: It goes to the south and turns about to the north; or: turning, turning about, the spirit goes, and returns to its circuits. From this we can reckon that in winter the sun runs to the southern quarter, in summer to the north, and thence by the equinox has the beginning of autumn; but the first breath, when the west wind grows warm, because in spring all things burst into bearing. But when he says: turning, turning about, the spirit goes, and returns to its circuits, either he has named the sun itself “spirit”, because it is a living thing and breathes and thrives and fulfils its yearly rounds by its course, as the poet says: “Meanwhile the sun rolls round the great year”; or because “the spirit within nourishes the shining globe of the moon and the Titanian stars, and mind, poured through the limbs, stirs the whole mass”, etc. He speaks not of the sun’s yearly course but of its daily paths; for by a slanting and broken line it goes through the south to the north, and so returns to the east.
29_marg634: He calls the sun itself the spirit, which animates and breathes into and quickens all things, as we see every year in the spring, which is thought to be the beginning of the world. 29_marg639: Jerome. He seems to speak of the things he counted up above, namely the mass of the lands, the rising and setting of the sun, the course of the rivers, the greatness of the ocean, and all the things we speak of by thought or sight or hearing: that nothing is new in nature. For from the beginning men have been born and died, and the earth been poised upon the waters, and the sun risen and set, and to birds it has been granted by God the maker to fly, to fishes to swim, and to the rest their own powers. Like this the comic poet says: “Nothing is said that has not been said before.” In expounding which Donatus said: “Perish those who said our things before us.” If it is so in speech, how much more in the governing of the world, which from the beginning of the age was so perfected that God rested from all his works on the seventh day.
29_marg640: What is it, etc. Of the natures created in the beginning of the world, and of their succession, how they come and pass: as a man dies, a man is born; the nature of the one born is the same that was of the one dying. So of birds, fishes, serpents and all living things; so of grasses, trees and other natures: nothing new is found which was not before, nothing past which is not afterwards done. Whence: “God rested on the seventh day from all his work”: from the creation of new natures, not from governing, according to that: “My Father worketh until now; and I work.” So from the first seeds of things the time of the whole world is carried through by a natural course.
29_marg641: Truly nothing is new, because it cannot be said: Behold this is new. “For it hath already gone before”, etc. Nor let us think that the signs and wonders and many things which are done new in the world by the will of God were already in former ages, and give room to Epicurus, who affirms that through countless periods the same things are done in these places and by the same persons. Otherwise Judas too has often betrayed, and Christ has often suffered for us, and the other things which have been done and are to come will likewise roll round into the same periods. But it is to be said that by the foreknowledge and predestination of God the things which are to come have already been done.
29_marg642: For it hath already, etc. As forgetfulness hides from us the past things that were of old, so those who are to be born will not be able to know the things that are done now; for they will perish in silence and be hidden as if they had not been. For it is vanity of vanities, and all is vanity, because all things pass in the manner of flowing water and will not return; to which sentence the whole world, and above all the human race, cries assent.
29_marg643: Jerome. The seraphim cover the face and feet of God because the first and the last things are covered. According to the Seventy: There is no remembrance for the first, and indeed for the last which are to be; there is no remembrance with those who will be at the last. The same in the Gospel: “The first shall be last, and the last first”, etc. And because God, as kind and merciful, remembers even all the least, to those who have deserved to be last he will not give so great glory as to those who, humbling themselves, have willed to be last in the world. Whence afterwards: “There shall be no remembrance of the wise no more than of the fool for ever.”

29_marg644: And I proposed, etc., as far as: hath God given to the children, etc. Like which is: “Wherefore God delivered them up to a reprobate sense”, that is, permitted them to be delivered up. Ecclesiastes, then, first of all set his heart to search for wisdom, wishing beyond what is lawful to know the causes and reasons why little ones are seized by a demon, why the godly and the ungodly are sunk in a like shipwreck; whether these things and the like come by chance or by the judgement of God. Desiring to know these things, he says, I understood that a superfluous care, tormenting through divers things, was given by God to men, so that they long to know what is not lawful; and this on account of their curiosity, into which they ran of their own accord.

29_marg648: I have seen, etc. I considered all worldly things, and saw that they are vanity and malice, that is, miseries of spirit, by which the mind, wearied with divers thoughts, labours to know what is not granted to man.
29_marg649: The word re‘ut Aquila and Theodotion rendered nomē, Symmachus boskēsis; the Seventy expressed it from the Syriac, not the Hebrew, saying proairesis. Nomē and boskēsis are words from pasturing, and proairesis sounds rather like “will” than “presumption”. And it is said that each one does what he wills and what seems right to him, and men are borne in divers directions by free choice, and all things under the sun are vain while we displease one another in the bounds of evil and good. A certain Hebrew told me that re‘ut in this place signifies affliction and malice rather than pasturing and will; not malice from evil as the contrary of good, but according to that: “Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof”; which the Greeks more expressively call kakōsis. And the sense is: I considered all things that are done in the world, and found nothing else but vanity and malices, that is, miseries of spirit, by which the soul is afflicted with divers thoughts.

29_marg650: Jerome. The perverse cannot be adorned, and the lacking cannot be numbered. For he who is perverse, unless he is first corrected, cannot be adorned: straight things are adorned, crooked ones corrected. This is against the heretics who bring in certain natures that cannot receive health. And because the lacking, that is, what is missing, cannot be numbered: only the firstborn of Israel were numbered; but the women and slaves and little ones and the rabble from Egypt, as not the fullness but the lack of the host, are not numbered. It can also be understood so: there is so much malice in the world that it cannot return to the whole state in which it was created. Otherwise: when all have been restored to wholeness through penance, the devil alone will remain in his error; for all things that are under the sun have been overthrown by his will and malignity, while sins are heaped up at his prompting. 29_marg653: I said, etc. Jerome. “Come now, I will try thee with mirth, and see good; and behold, this also is vanity.” After I found that in the multitude of wisdom and the addition of knowledge there was grief and labour, and nothing else but a fall and a struggle without end, I turned myself to mirth, to flow with luxury, to gather wealth, to abound in riches and to pluck perishing pleasures before I died; but in this I saw vanity, since past pleasure does not delight even in the present, and, once drained, does not satisfy. Not only bodily mirth but also spiritual is a temptation to him who has it, so that I need to be checked by “a sting of my flesh, an angel of Satan, to buffet me”, lest I be lifted up. Whence Solomon: “Give me neither beggary, nor riches”, and at once he adds: “lest perhaps being filled, I should be tempted to deny, and say: Who is the Lord?” Did not the devil too fall through an abundance of good things? Whence the Apostle: “lest being puffed up with pride, he fall into the judgement of the devil”, that is, into such a judgement as the devil also fell into. We can also call spiritual mirth vanity, like the rest, because we now see it through a glass in a dark manner; but when face to face, then it will be not vanity but truth.

29_marg654: Laughter, etc. Jerome. “Of laughter I said, Madness; and of mirth, What doth it?” Where we say “madness”, in the Hebrew is holel, which according to Aquila is “error”, according to Symmachus “tumult”; for which the Seventy and Theodotion have periphora, which can be rendered “a going round”. 29_marg716: It is better, etc. Because above we set out some people’s understanding of the place as of Christ, let us turn the rest too in the same order. It is better that two be together than one. For it is better to have Christ dwelling in oneself than to lie open alone to the snares of the adversary. For if one falls, Christ raises up his partner. Woe to him who, when he has fallen, has not Christ to raise him. If one sleeps, namely in death, and has Christ with him, he is warmed and quickened and comes back to life the sooner; and if the devil, fighting against him, presses on him strongly, the man will stand, and Christ for his man; not that the power of Christ is weak against the devil, but that free choice is left to man, and, when we are falling, he himself is stronger in the battle than we. But if the Father too and the Son and the Holy Ghost have come, this firmness is not quickly broken. But what is not easily broken is yet sometimes broken, as in Judas. For in Judas there was a threefold cord, but because after the morsel Satan entered into him, it was broken. And as for what is said above: if two sleep, they shall be warmed by each other, we take an example from Eliseus, who stretched himself upon the child and slept, and warmed his little body, and so gave him life as he rose. 29_marg721: Origen and Victorinus do not differ much from each other. The poor and wise child is Christ. Whence: “It is a great thing for thee to be called my servant [child]”; poor too, because “being rich, he became poor for us”; wise, because “he advanced in wisdom and age”. He was born in the kingdom of the old man, and therefore he says: “My kingdom is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly strive that I should not be delivered to the Jews: but now my kingdom is not from hence.” In the kingdom, then, of that old and foolish one, who showed him all the kingdoms of the world and their glory, the best child was born; and out of the house of the bound, of whom Jeremias: “To crush under his feet all the prisoners of the land”, he went forth to a kingdom, and went into a far country, and against those who would not have him reign, after a little time returned as king. Ecclesiastes, then, saw in the spirit all the living who can be partakers of the young man who says: “I am the life”, leaving the old foolish king to follow Christ. Likewise two peoples of Israel are signified: the former, which was before the coming, and the latter, which is to receive Antichrist in place of Christ; the former of which was not wholly cast off. For the first Church was gathered from the Jews and the apostles; and at the end the Jews who are to receive Antichrist in place of Christ will not rejoice in Christ.

29_marg812: Amos stood upon a plastered wall. And the Lord said to him: “What seest thou, Amos?” “A mason’s trowel”: I see it plastering the wall. In a trowel three things are considered: the edge, the wood and the flat. By the edge hard things are thrown off; by the wood things standing out are pressed in; by the flat all things are levelled and smoothed. A wall is made of smoothed and unsmoothed stones and mortar. This wall is the whole universe of the world, whose order and diversity consists in the variety of things. As in a wall some things lie hidden and some stand out, yet all are made level, so in the world some things that lie hidden come forth to their rising, and those that are at their setting tend to it and set; yet all are closed and levelled in one end. Upon this wall, that is, upon this variety and diversity, Amos stood, always stretching forth in mind to the things before. But Solomon stood under or beside this wall, and not above it; at length, considering with subtle inquiry the variety and changeableness of things, he understood that all things are vain and perishing. For the learned dies with the unlearned, the poor with the rich, and the like. And, as was said at the beginning, he put forth three volumes, the Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Canticle of Canticles, in which he portrays three kinds of men: beginners, those making progress, and the perfect. Hence he was called by three names: Jedidiah, that is, beloved; Ecclesiastes, that is, preacher; Solomon, that is, peaceable. In the title of the Parables he calls himself the son of the king of Israel, for there he speaks to greater and lesser, to beginners and the untaught, and to many. But in Ecclesiastes, the son of the king of Jerusalem: here he speaks now to those who have advanced, and to few. In the Canticle he calls himself only Solomon: there he speaks to the perfect and his equals. In the manner of a good orator, in this book he speaks to a people now repenting.
29_marg813: For Solomon is read to have offended God above all who were of his age in his time, and so much that he became an idolater for the love of women and built temples to three idols about Jerusalem; whence he is also said to have burnt incense. The Hebrews hand down that he repented, and in that repentance composed this book, in which he shows that all things are vain and perishing, and so by his own example calls them back from the error of vices and sins to penance. Its matter is the mason’s trowel, that is, the changeableness of the world, as has been said. Its intention is to call us back from the desire of worldly things to the contempt of them, so that with Amos we may stand not under or beside the wall but upon it. Its manner is this: in the prophetic way he sets first a preface, in which he shows who he is who speaks and to whom he speaks. It is to be noted too that not all the sentences set down here are Solomon’s, but various men’s. For this would not befit one so wise, namely: it is good that a man should drink and eat; and that: the death of men and of beasts is one; and that: what hath the wise man more than the fool? etc. So, having set down the opinions of various men, in the manner of a good preacher who, that all may hear him, calls for silence with his hand, he proclaims his own sentence, which all cry out to hold firmly. So: Let us all hear together the conclusion of the discourse. Fear God, and keep his commandments. This is, etc.
